items.text: Locating ourselves, without judgement — then the single idea that changes everything.
Not to judge — we all use all three. Just to notice where we tend to go.
Control
Permissive

items.def: Rewards and punishments to manage behaviour. Fast in the short term; over time it can erode trust and teach children to hide.

items.text: Avoids conflict, drops boundaries. Children feel loved but not safe — boundaries are part of safety.
Warm AND firm. Boundaries stay, held with empathy, while we stay curious about what's driving the behaviour.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 1
Control-based methods often work at first — which is exactly why they're so sticky.

items.def:
They manage the surface behaviour but leave the reason untouched.
They can teach children to avoid getting caught rather than to change.
Fear narrows a child's capacity to think and learn (more on this in Module 2).
The relationship — our real source of influence — quietly wears thin.
Under pressure, most of us default here. That's human, not a failing.

items.text: We're not swapping firm for soft. We're keeping the boundary and changing what surrounds it.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 1
Behaviour is communication. A child ‘acting out’ is acting out a feeling or need they can't yet put into words.
Your child screams and throws their plate at dinner. The ‘alarm’ is blaring. What do we do with an alarm?
Shouting at the alarm

items.def:
Focus on the noise: ‘Stop that RIGHT now!’
Punish the plate-throwing itself.
Alarm may quiet — but the fire still burns.

lines: Ask: what's this behaviour telling me?
Notice: overtired? overwhelmed? disconnected?
Address the cause — the alarm can finally rest.

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 1
The same moment, approached two completely different ways.

items.def:
A judge asks: ‘What did they do, and what do they deserve?’
A detective asks: ‘What happened for them, and what do they need?’
The judge closes the case; the detective stays curious.
Curiosity keeps the relationship open — and open relationships are where change happens.
This is the mindset we'll practise for six weeks.

items.text: For the rest of today, catch yourself judging — and gently switch to wondering instead.

items.def:
Above the surface: the behaviour (hitting, refusing, screaming, lying).
Below: the FEELING — scared, ashamed, powerless, jealous, overwhelmed.
Below: the NEED — safety, connection, control, rest, food, predictability.
Below: what they can't YET do — wait, share, calm down, use words.
Below: the BODY — fight, flight, or freeze.

items.text: A simple, physical model of what's happening when a child (or a parent) loses it.

sections.label: SIEGEL'S HAND MODEL
sections.heading: Make a fist — that's the brain

items.text: Tuck your thumb into your palm and fold your fingers over it.
Wrist / palm
Thumb inside

items.def: The brainstem — survival, heartbeat, breathing, and the fight / flight / freeze alarm.

items.text: The limbic brain — feelings, memory, attachment, and the amygdala ‘smoke alarm’.
The cortex — thinking, empathy, impulse control. The very front is the wise leader.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 2
Someone says the thing that really gets you. Whoosh — the fingers fly up off the thumb. That's flipping your lid.
Lid flipped (survival brain)

items.def:
The thinking brain goes offline.
Reason, logic, and empathy switch off.
The survival brain runs the show.

lines: You can't talk sense to a flipped lid.
The part that hears sense has left.
First bring the lid down — then talk.

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 2

sections.label: DEVELOPMENT TAKES TIME
sections.heading: The brain builds from the bottom up

items.text: Survival first, feelings next, thinking last — and ‘last’ takes decades.

items.def:
The brainstem is ready at birth; the thinking cortex is barely begun.
The prefrontal cortex isn't fully wired until the mid-twenties.
Expecting adult self-control from a child is expecting fruit from a sapling.
‘Why can't they just calm down?’ — often, the machinery to do that isn't built yet.
Our job is to be the borrowed thinking brain until theirs matures.

items.text: Much ‘won't’ is actually ‘can't yet’. That single word changes how we respond.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 2

sections.label: THE ORDER THAT ACTUALLY WORKS (BRUCE PERRY)
sections.heading: Regulate → Relate → Reason

items.text: Try to reason first and it bounces off. This is the sequence that lands.
Regulate  — calm the body first, yours and theirs. No learning happens in survival mode.

items.def: Relate  — connect: warm tone, get close, be present. Safety is felt before it's understood.
Reason  — only now can you problem-solve, teach, or set the lesson. The thinking brain is back.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 2

items.text: Your child melts down over the ‘wrong’ colour cup. Same juice, different cup. Their lid is up.
Reason first (it fails)

items.def:
‘It's exactly the same juice!’
Explaining harder, getting louder.
The meltdown grows — logic can't land.

lines: Calm presence, fewer words, soft voice.
Get low, warm, close.
Later: ‘Shall we pick cups together tomorrow?’

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 2

lines: When YOUR lid flips, what's the very first sign in your body?

sections.label: OUR ‘GREEN ZONE’
sections.heading: What is the window of tolerance?

items.text: A band of arousal where we're calm enough to think and connected enough to cope.

items.def:
Inside the window: regulated, curious, able to learn and cooperate.
This is the only zone where teaching, reasoning, and connection actually work.
Push out of the top or bottom and the thinking brain goes offline again.
Everyone has a window — children's are simply narrower and still growing.
Our calm presence is what widens a child's window over time.

items.text: We're not trying to stop big feelings. We're helping children spend more time in the green zone — and return to it faster.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 2

sections.label: TWO WAYS TO LEAVE THE GREEN ZONE
sections.heading: Above and below the window

items.text: Above — hyperarousal

items.def:
Fight or flight: too much energy
Shouting, hitting, running, panic
‘Too big’ feelings spilling over
Looks like: defiance, aggression, chaos

lines: Freeze or shutdown: too little energy
Going quiet, floppy, blank, withdrawn
‘Switched off’, not present
Looks like: sulking, ‘ignoring’, spacing out

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 2
Beneath awareness, the nervous system is always asking one question.

items.def:
Neuroception: the body constantly scans — ‘Am I safe, or in danger?’ — below conscious thought.
A child who feels safe has a wide window; a stressed child tips out fast.
We send safety cues through our face, voice, and body — often before words.
‘Name it to tame it’: putting words to a feeling helps calm the emotional brain.
‘You're really disappointed’ can settle a storm faster than any explanation.

items.text: Next storm, narrate the feeling instead of fixing the problem: ‘That was so frustrating.’

items.text: Yesterday your child handled the supermarket beautifully. Today, tired and hungry, the same trip ends in tears.

items.def: ‘Their window is narrow today’

lines: Read it as choice or manipulation.
Respond with a consequence.
The window narrows further; it escalates.
Read it as capacity, not character.
Reduce demands; meet the basic need.
Rest, food, predictability widen the window.

sections.label: BOWLBY & AINSWORTH
sections.heading: Two jobs of a secure attachment

items.text: Secure base

items.def: A launchpad to explore the world from. Because you've got their back, they dare to venture out.

items.text: Somewhere to run back to when the world gets too big. The harbour, always open.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 3

sections.label: SERVE AND RETURN
sections.heading: Built in a thousand small moments

items.text: Attachment isn't built in grand gestures — it's built in tiny exchanges, all day long.

items.def:
The baby babbles, we babble back. The toddler shows a stone, we look.
Each exchange says: ‘I see you. You're worth responding to.’
Thousands of these moments wire a child's sense of being loved and safe.
We miss plenty of them — and that's completely fine.
Attunement doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to be frequent enough, and repaired.

items.text: You don't have to catch every serve. You just have to keep playing the game.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 3
Children's coping patterns are clever survival strategies — not flaws, and not labels to pin on a child.

sections.label: WHY PATTERNS FORM
sections.heading: When connection can't be counted on

items.text: A child who isn't sure a caregiver will respond doesn't give up — they adapt, cleverly, to get what they can.
How it can look

items.def:
Some amplify: louder, bigger, harder to ignore.
Some minimise: quiet, self-reliant, ‘no bother’.
Easy to misread as ‘drama’ or ‘coldness’.

lines: An intelligent bid to stay connected and safe.
A strategy that fit the situation, not a defect.
Softens with reliable, attuned care over time.

sections.label: LINKING BACK
sections.heading: PACE delivers the first three S's

items.text: Safe, Seen, Soothed → Secure. Here's how we make a child feel each one.
How a child feels Safe

items.def: By our calm, predictable, non-frightening presence — even in conflict.

items.text: By our curiosity about their inner world: ‘I wonder what that was like for you.’
How a child feels Soothed

items.def: By our empathy and co-regulation when feelings get too big.

items.text: The three above, repeated enough times, become a deep sense of ‘I can rely on this.’

sections.label: THE WHOLE STANCE AT A GLANCE
sections.heading: PACE — four elements

items.text: Playfulness

items.def: A warm, light tone that says ‘our bond is bigger than this problem’. Never to mock or dodge real feelings.

items.text: Every feeling is allowed, even while behaviour has limits. Accept the feeling; limit the action.
Curiosity

items.def: Wonder aloud about what's underneath — ‘I wonder if…’ — with genuine, non-judgemental interest.

items.text: Stay alongside the feeling rather than rushing to fix it. Feeling felt is what regulates.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 3

sections.label: ACCEPT THE FEELING, LIMIT THE BEHAVIOUR
sections.heading: Acceptance: the hardest one

items.text: ‘I HATE you! I'm not going to bed!’ Acceptance means welcoming the feeling while still holding the limit.
Rejecting the feeling

items.def:
‘Don't you dare speak to me like that.’
‘You don't hate me, stop being silly.’
The child feels wrong for feeling.

lines: ‘You're allowed to be furious with me.’
‘It's still bedtime — and that anger is okay.’
The feeling is safe; the boundary holds.

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 3
Bedtime resistance every single night. Instead of a battle, we get curious — with the child, not about them.
Assuming & correcting

items.def:
‘You're just stalling. Bed. Now.’
A verdict, delivered.
The real reason stays hidden.

lines: ‘I wonder if bedtime feels scary when it goes quiet.’
‘I'm not cross — I'm just wondering with you.’
The child feels seen; the reason surfaces.

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 3
The two elements that keep connection alive through the hard bits.

items.def:
Playfulness lowers defences: ‘Uh-oh, the sock monster struck again!’
It says the relationship is bigger than the problem — used lightly, never to belittle distress.
Empathy stays alongside: ‘That was so disappointing. I'm right here.’
Empathy doesn't fix or explain — it simply joins the child in the feeling.
Feeling felt, not fixed, is what actually settles a nervous system.

items.text: Playfulness fits some moments; empathy fits almost all of them. When in doubt, lead with empathy.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 3
‘I wonder if you're feeling this. That makes sense. I'm right here with you.’ — curiosity, acceptance, and empathy, in one breath.
In trios (parent / child / observer), rework a common scenario first the ‘old way’, then with PACE.
Pick a scenario: won't leave the park; ‘I hate you!’; won't do homework; hit a sibling.

items.def: Round 1: respond correct-first, as many of us instinctively do. Notice how the ‘child’ feels.
Round 2: lead with one or two PACE elements. The observer notes what shifts.
Swap roles if time allows, then debrief out of role.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 3

lines: How did being met with acceptance feel in the child role?
Which PACE element came most naturally? Which felt hardest?
What changed in the room between round one and round two?

items.def: The words matter less than the felt sense of ‘I'm with you.’ PACE is a stance you return to, not lines you recite.

items.text: Why a child's storm settles when — and only when — an adult stays calm enough to lend it.
Children aren't born able to calm themselves. They learn it by borrowing ours, thousands of times.

items.def:
Self-regulation is built from countless experiences of being co-regulated.
A calm adult nervous system literally settles a distressed child's.
We lend calm through steady breathing, soft eyes, a warm voice, a still body.
This isn't soft or indulgent — it's how the brain wires the capacity to self-soothe.
Every time you stay calm with them, you're building a circuit they'll use for life.

items.text: You're not just ending today's storm — you're teaching the brain how storms end.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 4

sections.label: RIDE IT, DON'T FIGHT IT
sections.heading: Every big feeling is a wave

items.text: Emotions have a shape: they rise, they crest, and they fall. All of them.

items.def:
On the way up, energy and distress build fast.
At the crest, the thinking brain is fully offline.
On the way down, the child can gradually reconnect and reflect.
The single most useful rule: don't try to teach at the peak.
Ride the wave with presence — the lesson comes later, in the calm.

items.text: Presence, not problem-solving. Your job is to be the calm shore, not to explain the tide.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 4
Tantrum

items.def:
Has a goal (‘I want the sweet’)
Often checks for an audience
Thinking brain partly online
Respond: calm warmth + hold the boundary

lines: No goal — pure overwhelm
Doesn't care who's watching
Thinking brain fully offline
Respond: safety, fewer words, quiet presence

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 4

sections.label: THE SAME BEHAVIOUR, TWO DIFFERENT NEEDS
sections.heading: Reading the moment

items.text: Your child is on the floor screaming in the shop. Is this a tantrum or a meltdown? The response depends on the answer.
If it's a tantrum

items.def:
‘I know — you really wanted it.’
‘The answer's still no. I'm right here.’
Warm, connected, boundary firmly held.

lines: Fewer words, lower voice, less stimulation.
Safety and quiet presence — no lecturing.
Just help the wave pass; talk later.

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 4
You can't reason a child out of a meltdown. You can only keep them safe and lend them your calm until the wave passes.

lines: Think of a recent storm. Was it more tantrum or meltdown — and how can you tell?
What do you tend to reach for at the peak? Does it help the wave pass, or prolong it?

items.text: A few minutes each. Be gentle with yourself — most of us were never taught this.
Move, stretch, get a drink. Movement helps our own nervous systems settle — model what we're teaching.
A simple, ordered set of rungs to climb in the moment — starting, always, with yourself.

sections.label: IN THE HEAT OF THE MOMENT
sections.heading: The five-step regulation ladder

items.text: Order matters — each rung depends on the one below it.

items.def: 1 · Regulate yourself  — breathe out slowly, drop your shoulders, soften your voice. You are the thermostat.
2 · Reduce the load  — fewer words, lower voice, less stimulation, clear the audience, find a quieter spot.
3 · Connect  — get to their level; offer warm presence and proximity. Safety is felt through your body first.
4 · Co-regulate & name  — soothe with rhythm and breath; gently name the feeling: ‘This is so hard. I've got you.’
5 · Reflect — later  — once the wave has passed and the thinking brain is back, revisit, make sense, repair, plan.

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 4
Your child is melting down and you feel your own lid starting to flip. Everything hinges on this next moment.
Two flooded systems

items.def:
You match their volume and intensity.
Two dysregulated brains amplify each other.
The storm doubles instead of settling.

lines: You fit your own oxygen mask first.

Simple, repeated, low-demand phrases — offered calmly, not as a script to rush through.

items.def:
‘You're safe. I'm here.’
‘You don't have to talk. We'll just breathe together.’
‘This is a big wave. It will pass. I'm not going anywhere.’
‘I've got you.’
Fewer words, more presence — your tone carries more than the content.

items.text: You're not trying to end the feeling. You're making sure they're not alone in it.

items.text: Respond to the reason, not just the act — and understand why the old tools so often disappoint.
A behaviour is a hidden reason meeting the child's current capacity to cope.

items.def:
Change what you can reach — the reason and the capacity — and behaviour follows.
Punish only the surface and the reason simply finds another exit.
The same behaviour can have completely different reasons on different days.
Our first question is no longer ‘How do I stop this?’ but ‘What is this about?’
This doesn't drop the boundary — it aims it at the right target.

items.text: From ‘What's wrong with this child?’ to ‘What happened, and what do they need?’

Fear & anxiety

items.def: Including the fear of getting it wrong, or of losing your approval.

items.text: Feeling bad about oneself — a huge, under-recognised driver of behaviour.
A need for control

items.def: When life feels unpredictable, children grab control wherever they can.

items.text: Sensory overload, hunger, tiredness, illness — so often the real cause.

items.def: A skill not yet learned

items.text: ‘Are you still there for me?’ — behaviour as a bid for connection.
Waiting, sharing, calming, using words — still under construction.

‘Attention-seeking’ is really connection-seeking. And a child seeking connection needs connection — not withdrawal.
Rewards and punishments assume the thinking brain is in the driver's seat. Often, it isn't.

items.def:
They assume the child COULD behave and is simply choosing not to.
A child in survival mode can't access the machinery to weigh consequences.
Punishment adds fear, which narrows the window and fuels the next incident.
Rewards can make love and approval feel conditional on performance.
None of this means ‘no boundaries’ — it means boundaries held through relationship, not fear.

items.text: For a regulated, capable child, simple rewards can be fine. The problem is using them on a flooded one.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 5
Natural & logical consequences

items.def:
Natural: flow from the act (throw the toy, it breaks)
Logical: connected & reasonable (paint the wall, clean it together)
Delivered WITH empathy and connection
Teach cause and repair

lines: Imposed to make the child ‘pay’
Unrelated to the act, and shaming
Delivered with anger or withdrawal
Teaches fear, not learning

The same five moves, whatever the behaviour.

items.def: 1 · Regulate  — yourself first (Module 4). No useful response starts from a flipped lid.
2 · Connect  — warmth and presence before words. Reach the child, not just the behaviour.
3 · Understand  — name the likely reason beneath: ‘I think you're scared / tired / needing control.’
4 · Boundary with empathy  — hold the limit AND the relationship: ‘I won't let you… and I'm here.’
5 · Teach or repair — later  — once calm, make sense of it together and plan for next time.

items.text: Usually fear-driven. Make truth safe: ‘You won't be in trouble for telling me the truth.’ Name the wish behind the lie.

items.def: Coach, don't referee. Don't hunt a culprit — name both children's feelings and keep everyone safe.

items.text: The most freeing idea in the course — and the distinction that protects your child from the inside out.
Rupture is normal and not harmful. It's UNrepaired rupture that wounds — and repair is a gift, not just damage control.
Repairing after a rupture doesn't just undo harm — it actively teaches.

items.def:
It teaches that relationships survive conflict and anger.
It teaches that your child is still loved after a hard moment.
By watching you own your part, they learn how to take responsibility.
It models humility, accountability, and emotional honesty.
The rupture-repair cycle itself builds resilience — you don't need to avoid all rupture.

items.text: You don't have to never lose it. You have to come back and repair when you do.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 6
Simple, sincere, and short — not a grovelling performance.

items.def: 1 · Regulate yourself  — find your own calm before you approach. Don't repair from a still-flipped lid.
2 · Reconnect  — warmth first: a soft look, sitting close, a gentle tone.
3 · Own your part  — ‘I shouted, and that wasn't okay. I'm sorry.’ Clean, without excuses.
4 · Name what happened  — briefly make sense of it together: ‘We both got overwhelmed.’
5 · Move forward  — reassure the bond: ‘Nothing you do stops me loving you.’

items.text: Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 6
Guilt — bearable, useful

items.def:
‘I did something bad.’
About the behaviour
Motivates repair and change
We can gently support it

lines: ‘I AM bad.’
About the whole self
Drives hiding, lying, rage, disconnection
Fuels the very behaviours we're trying to help

sections.label: SEPARATE THE CHILD FROM THE BEHAVIOUR
sections.heading: Reducing shame

items.text: Your child does something genuinely unkind. They need to know it's not okay — without absorbing ‘I am a bad person.’
Shaming the child

items.def:
‘You're so mean / bad / naughty.’
Withdraw love; send them away to feel it.
The message: I am bad, and I'm alone.

lines: ‘You're a good kid who made a bad choice.’
Stay close; address the act, keep the bond.
Bring PACE — accept the child, limit the act.

sections.label: TEACHING BLOCK 2
sections.heading: The long game & caring for you

items.text: Perfection is off the table — and thank goodness. What sustains this is ‘good enough’, and a parent who's looked after.
The research is genuinely liberating on this point.

items.def:
We're attuned to our children only about a third of the time — and that's enough.
It's the cycle of misattunement and repair, not flawless attunement, that builds security.
A ‘good enough’ parent is present and repairing, not perfect.
Trying to be perfect actually models anxiety and fragility.
You are allowed to be a work in progress in front of your child.

items.text: You don't need to be a perfect parent. You need to be a present, repairing one.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 6

sections.label: PLAYING THE LONG GAME
sections.heading: Progress is not a straight line

items.text: Change in a family is real, but it rarely looks like steady, tidy improvement.

items.def:
Expect setbacks — around change, transitions, illness, tiredness, big events.
A hard week after a good one is not failure; it's how change actually looks.
Zoom out: track the month, not the moment.
Celebrate small wins loudly — they're the real evidence.
This is a marathon of thousands of small moments of safety. They're landing, even unseen.

items.text: Most of the change you're creating, you'll never directly see. Trust it anyway.
Therapeutic Parenting   ·   Module 6

sections.label: YOU CAN'T POUR FROM AN EMPTY CUP
sections.heading: Caring for the parent

items.text: Self-compassion

items.def: Talk to yourself as you would to a struggling friend. This isn't indulgence — it's fuel.

items.text: When we're depleted or triggered, our warmth can switch off. Rest and support switch it back on.
Ghosts in the nursery

items.def: Our own childhood gets stirred up by our children. Noticing our triggers frees us to respond to now.

items.text: Getting your own support isn't a luxury — it's part of the parenting.

You cannot pour from an empty cup. Looking after yourself is not a break from the parenting — it is the parenting.
